messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 23
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Urban Planner
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kofi's Story

Kofi was twenty-three when the assault happened, a young urban planner with a growing portfolio of transit redesigns and a life that felt, for the first time, genuinely his own. He had moved to the city six months earlier, renting a small apartment in a neighbourhood he was helping to revitalize. On a Friday night in March, he stopped at a corner store near his building. He was reaching for bottled water when three men entered. What followed was fragmented in his mind now—a flash of movement, a voice thick with alcohol, a fist. The smell of whiskey and sweat filled his nostrils as he was shoved against the cooler. His wallet was gone in seconds. The police arrived twenty minutes later. When Kofi tried to explain what had happened, the words would not come; he could see the moment the first man's jaw clenched, could picture the bottle glinting under the fluorescent lights, but the sequence dissolved into isolated snapshots, each one vivid and senseless. The officers took his statement with visible impatience, filed a report, and told him they would be in touch. They never were.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi returned to work, but something fundamental had shifted. The office building where he spent his days—a glass structure with open-plan floors—became a minefield. Any unexpected sound made him flinch violently; the scrape of a chair, a door closing down the corridor, even the ping of an arriving email could send his heart racing as though the assault were happening again. When a colleague raised her voice during a meeting—nothing hostile, just animated discussion of a zoning proposal—Kofi felt his body flood with panic, as if danger were imminent. He began avoiding meetings where conflict might arise, declining to present his own ideas if there was any chance of disagreement. The avoidance provided momentary relief, but it also meant that his work suffered; he was sidelined from a major project, passed over for presentations. Each trigger—the smell of alcohol on a commuter's breath, a sudden movement in his peripheral vision, the sound of someone's raised voice—sent him spiralling into a state of hypervigilance that left him exhausted and convinced that nowhere was truly safe, no matter what anyone told him.

The memory of the assault haunted him in discrete, overwhelming moments. When the images surfaced—the attacker's expression, the cold of the metal cooler against his back—Kofi was flooded with such intense emotion that he could not function. He would have to leave his desk, lock himself in a bathroom stall, wait for the panic to subside. These intrusions were unpredictable, arriving without warning, and they fed a growing conviction that he was fundamentally broken, unable to cope with even minor stressors. The assault had revealed to him a truth he could not escape: the institutions meant to protect him had failed. The police had done nothing. His employer had no real support for trauma. He was alone. This belief—that he could not handle what life threw at him, that no one and nothing could be trusted to keep him safe—began to color everything. When the memory surfaced, it reinforced his sense of helplessness; when he encountered a trigger, it seemed to confirm that the world was genuinely dangerous and he was powerless to prevent harm.

Over the following months, Kofi developed ways to manage the unbearable feelings. He began gambling—first online poker, then visiting a casino on weekends—drawn to the distraction and the rush of possibility, however brief. Gambling became a escape from the rumination that otherwise consumed him. He would lie awake at night replaying the assault, convinced that he should have done something differently, that his failure to fight back or run was a personal weakness. The self-blame was relentless. Yet when he tried to stop gambling, when he attempted to sit with his thoughts, the memory would intrude again, and he would find himself back at the casino or scrolling through betting apps, seeking any distraction that might quieten the voice telling him he was powerless and broken. His avoidance of conflict deepened; he withdrew from friendships, turned down social invitations, and created a narrow, controlled life in which nothing unpredictable could happen. But this constriction itself became a source of shame and further self-blame. He had come to believe that his inability to cope—even with normal disagreement or unexpected sounds—was a personal failing, evidence that he lacked the resilience others possessed.

Now, three months into this cycle, Kofi sits in a therapist's office for the first time. His PCL-5 score of 77 reflects the severity of his distress. He is hoping, he says quietly, that someone might help him understand why he cannot simply move past this, why the world still feels so dangerous, and why he cannot trust that he will ever be safe again. What he fears most is that this is who he has become—a man who jumps at shadows, who cannot hold a job, who ruins his own life through gambling and avoidance. He is not sure he believes help is possible, but he is here because the alternative—continuing as he is—has become unbearable.
